rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction to be patient addresses the Prophet, or by extension all Muslims.
rows.anchor: The injunction Be patient is addressed to the Prophet or to all Muslims

rows.speaker: most scholars
rows.claim: Most understand the resolute messengers as Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad, who brought a new Book and revealed law.
rows.anchor: most often understood to mean the messengers who brought a new Book and a new revealed law from God

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Other proposals identify Noah, Hud, and Abraham, or all the prophets, as the resolute messengers.
rows.anchor: other proposals for the referent, ranging from three prophets—Noah, Hūd, and Abraham—to all the prophets (Q)

rows.speaker: al-Tustarī
rows.claim: Al-Tustari identifies twelve patient prophets as resolute, recounting the trials and steadfastness of Abraham, Job, Ishmael, Noah, Jonah, Joseph, and Jacob.
rows.anchor:
al-
Tustarī writes, “The resolute among the messengers are Abraham

rows.speaker: JJ, Q
rows.claim: The Prophet is told not to pray for the disbelievers' punishment to be hastened, as some prophets had done, because it would arrive in due course.
rows.anchor: not to pray for punishment to be hastened against the disbelievers, as some prophets had done in the past

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delay may be understood as God's mercy or as a means of reserving a greater punishment for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: This postponement can be understood as a mercy from God or to mean that God has a greater punishment for them in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reality and length of the Hereafter make worldly life seem to the disbelievers like only an hour of a day.
rows.anchor: the reality and duration of the Hereafter will make the life of this world seem for them as though they had tarried naught but an hour of a day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The iniquitous are destroyed through punishment in the Hereafter and by being led astray, made to forget God, and distanced from Him and their true selves.
rows.anchor: The iniquitous are destroyed by being punished in the Hereafter, but moreover by being led astray

rows.speaker: scholars
rows.claim: Scholars agree that Qaf is Makkan, though some classify verse 38 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: all scholars agree that Qāf is a Makkan sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is named for its opening Arabic letter and is also called al-Basiqat, “The Towering,” after the date palms in verse 10; its threat theme may be another title.
rows.anchor: known to some as al-Bāsiqāt, “The Towering,” after the reference to date palms towering with layered spathes in v. 10

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may be called the Surah of the Threat because four of the Quran's six uses of wa'id occur in it.
rows.anchor: six times that threat or “warning”

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The preceding surah criticizes people who claim faith without its fullness, while Qaf criticizes rejection of Muhammad's prophethood and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: this sūrah criticizes those who do not believe in the prophethood of Muhammad and the Hereafter (Āl)

rows.speaker: many scholars
rows.claim: Many scholars treat Qaf as the beginning of the separated, shorter surahs, where shorter length brings more frequent basmalahs.
rows.anchor: consider Qāf to mark the beginning of the“separated”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have recited Qaf from the pulpit during Friday congregational sermons in later years.
rows.anchor: in later years, the Prophet would recite Qāf from the pulpit during the sermon of the Friday congregational prayer

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is also reported to recite Qaf and al-Qamar at both feasts and often during the morning prayer.
rows.anchor: read Qāf and Sūrah 54, al-Qamar, during the

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: The Prophet's frequent recitation has led some to count Qaf among the greatest surahs.
rows.anchor: some to consider it as among the greatest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah moves from rejection of the Prophet and resurrection, through creation and past peoples, to death, the Hereafter, mindfulness of death, and a final reminder.
rows.anchor: the sūrah calls one to reflect upon the wonders of creation as evidence of God’s Omnipotence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to patience addresses the Prophet and, by extension, all Muslims, urging endurance of the chiding of disbelievers and naysayers.
rows.anchor: enjoins the Prophet and, by extension, all Muslims to bear patiently the chiding of disbelievers and naysayers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praising God means turning to Him instead of dwelling on disbelievers' words.
rows.anchor: one should not dwell upon the words of disbelievers, but instead turn to God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some commentators identify the time before sunrise as the morning prayer and before sunset as the late afternoon prayer.
rows.anchor: before the rising of the sun refers to the morning prayer and before the setting refers to the late afternoon prayer (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Other commentators say that “before the setting” refers to both afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: others say that before the setting refers to both afternoon prayers (JJ, Z)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: On a full-moon night, the Prophet told Companions that they would see their Lord as plainly as the moon and urged them not to miss the dawn and afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said to a group of his Companions, “You will see your Lord as you see this moon

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: All commentators classify al-Waqiah as Makkan, though some place verses 81–82 or verse 83 in the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: commentators consider al-Wāqiʿah to be a Makkan sūrah

rows.speaker: a minority
rows.claim: A minority say verses 39–40 were revealed during the Prophet's migration from Makkah to Madinah.
rows.anchor: A minority consider vv. 39–40 to have been revealed during the Prophet’s emigration from Makkah to Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its name from the Event in verse 1, meaning the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: takes its name from the mention of the Event in v. 1, a reference to the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its central theme is the Hereafter's fate for the foremost, companions of the right, and companions of the left; it continues and completes al-Rahman by contrasting Paradise's blessings with Hell's punishments.
rows.anchor: this sūrah can be seen as a continuation and completion of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Five overlapping sections cover Judgment's signs, the three groups' destinies, proofs of resurrection, the revelation, and death and the Afterlife.
rows.anchor: The sūrah comprises five overlapping sections

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A well-known hadith promises that whoever recites al-Waqiah every night will never be afflicted by need.
rows.anchor: According to a well-known ḥadīth, “Whosoever recites Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah every night shall never be afflicted by need”

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn Ajibah explains the recitation's promised protection as arising because understanding the surah's teachings on the Hereafter prompts preparation for it.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah states that this is because whoever understands the things mentioned in this sūrah regarding the Hereafter will set about preparing for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This attributed virtue has made the surah widely recited at significant moments, especially for the dying or recently dead.
rows.anchor: one of the most often recited

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most take the particle la in fa-la uqsimu as emphatic, rendering the oath “I swear.”
rows.anchor: Most interpret it to function as the former

rows.speaker: Q, Sh, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some read la as negation: “Nay, I swear,” denouncing what opponents say before swearing.
rows.anchor: some see it as a particle of negation, in which case it would be translated, “Nay, I swear”

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The places where stars descend most likely means when, where, or how celestial bodies set, or their stations, as in other Quranic references.
rows.anchor: most likely refers to the time, place, or manner in which celestial bodies set or to the stations of the stars

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may refer to stars fading on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: It can also be taken as a reference to the fading of the stars on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: If it refers to stars setting, the oath alludes to night hours considered especially good for voluntary devotions.
rows.anchor: an allusion to the times of night that are thought to be best for supererogatory devotions

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Nujum can mean portions or installments, so the oath may refer to the Quran's gradual revelation in groups of three, four, or five verses over twenty-three years.
rows.anchor: an interpretation attributed to some early commentators who see this verse as a reference to the gradual revelation of the Quran

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The descending stars or Quranic installments may allude to their descent into the hearts of God's servants, angels, messengers, and righteous believers.
rows.anchor: an allusion to the hearts of God’s servants, angels, messengers, and the righteous among the believers

rows.speaker: Aj, R
rows.claim: With a grammatical stop after “oath,” the conditional “if you but knew” may imply that knowledge would lead one to affirm the oath, act on that knowledge, or strive for certainty.
rows.anchor: read by some with a full grammatical stop after oath

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: Some classify al-Hadid as Makkan, while most classify it as Madinan; Ibn Atiyyah suggests it contains Madinan verses but appears Makkan in its middle part.
rows.anchor: The sixth/twelfth-century commentator Ibn ʿAṭiyyah proposes a potential resolution to this dispute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hadid is named for the phrase “We sent down iron” in verse 25 and begins the five Glorifiers, along with surahs 59, 61, 62, and 64.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the phrase We sent down iron in v. 25

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says one verse among the Glorifiers is better than a thousand verses; some identify it as 57:3, others as the last verse of al-Hashr.
rows.anchor: Within [the Glorifiers] there is a verse that is better than a thousand verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's sections emphasize God's omnipresence and power, belief and spending, believers' and hypocrites' ends, worldly ephemerality and charity, and the People of the Book's relation to Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: The next five verses (vv. 7–11) then enjoin belief in God and spending one’s wealth in the way of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly wealth is relative, yet can be a cause for gratitude and should be managed properly.
rows.anchor: Such wealth is seen as a cause of gratitude and should be managed properly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Withering or failed crops serve elsewhere as metaphors for the relative and fleeting joys of worldly life.
rows.anchor: Crops that dry or fail are also used as a metaphor for the relativity of the joys of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kuffar, translated here as farmers, can also mean disbelievers and could be rendered that way in this passage.
rows.anchor: farmers translates kuffār, which can also mean “disbelievers” and could be rendered as such in this passage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that worldly life is delusive enjoyment is also found in other verses.
rows.anchor: For the life of this world is naught but the enjoyment of delusion, see also

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn Ajibah says the world looks beautiful outside but hides ugliness within, gradually entangling its pursuers until they neglect preparation for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah writes: “[The world] is something that appears beautiful on the outside, but that conceals what is ugly within it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion extends the surah's focus on the relationship between inward and outward appearances.
rows.anchor: The discussion of the deceptive nature of this world continues this sūrah’s focus upon the relationship between the inward and the outward

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hashr is Madinan, named for the first gathering in verse 2; it is also called al-Nadir or Banu Nadir because most verses are said to concern the tribe's expulsion for breaking its treaty.
rows.anchor: It is also known as al-Naḍīr or Banū Naḍīr (Āl, IJ, Ṭ), since most of its verses are said to have been revealed in relation to the Jewish tribe of Banū Naḍīr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is the second Glorifier; a hadith says a verse in the group is better than a thousand, identified by some as 57:3 and by others as al-Hashr's last verse.
rows.anchor: this ḥadīth refers to v. 3 of Sūrah 57, al-Ḥadīd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Madinah tribes' covenant pledged mutual defense against outside attack and prohibited alliances against one another.
rows.anchor: they pledged to support one another, should any of them be attacked by outside forces, and to make no alliances against one another

rows.speaker: the Muslims
rows.claim: After Badr, Muslims believed the Banu Qaynuqa had broken the covenant, and the tribe was expelled from the oasis.
rows.anchor: The Muslims believed that the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Uhud, the Banu Nadir were accused of allying against Muslims and plotting to kill the Prophet; reports say Gabriel or a Banu Nadir woman informed him.
rows.anchor: some say from the Archangel Gabriel, others say through a woman of the Banū Naḍīr

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet offered the Banu Nadir exile with their possessions and crop proceeds, or war; they asked for ten days to decide.
rows.anchor: the choice of leaving the oasis with all their possessions, but retaining the right to the proceeds from their crops, or facing war

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After consulting allies, including Madinah hypocrites, the Banu Nadir chose war, expecting reinforcements that never came.
rows.anchor: they chose the latter course, thinking that reinforcements would be forthcoming

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Muslim siege lasted twenty-one days with little fighting; cutting prized date palms led the Banu Nadir to accept exile.
rows.anchor: The Muslim armies besieged their fortresses for twenty-one days, during which time the fighting was limited to brief exchanges of arrows

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under the final settlement, the Banu Nadir could keep their wealth except arms but surrendered their land and crops.
rows.anchor: they would be banished, allowed to keep their considerable wealth, except their armaments, but had to forfeit their land, crops and all

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah addresses emigrants, Helpers who embraced Islam before and after the emigration, hypocrites, and Jewish tribes in the early Muslim community.
rows.anchor: this sūrah addresses all of the groups that were to be found in the nascent Muslim community

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah moves from the Banu Nadir to spoils and community relations, compares hypocrites' counsel with Satan's, contrasts Fire and Garden, then treats revelation and Divine Names.
rows.anchor: whose counsel toward one another is likened to that of Satan (v. 16)
